script.opening: (June starts the call, Edith beside her.) "Thank goodness I got through, doctor. Mum's been getting worse for two weeks — she's leaving the cooker on, she didn't recognise me on Sunday, and she's only picking at her food. I don't know what to do anymore." Then Edith says, vaguely: "I'm fine, I just had a bit of a funny turn."

facts.text: Two-week trajectory of worsening confusion. Day-to-day fluctuating — better in the morning, worse evenings.
Smelly urine for the past week, daughter has noticed. Edith brushes it off.
Started co-codamol 30/500 four weeks ago after a knee flare — prescribed by another GP.
Not drinking fluids — daughter says she gets one cup of tea down her in a day.
If GP gently probes June: she is the only carer, has not had a respite break in 8 months, is using her own pension to top up mother's food shop, and broke down in tears in the corridor last week.
One unwitnessed fall last Tuesday — no injury. Daughter found Edith on the floor of the bathroom.

ice.ideas: June thinks "it's dementia getting worse". Edith says "I'm fine".
ice.concerns: June is terrified mother will die at home alone before help arrives. She has not slept properly in a fortnight.
ice.expectations: June wants something doing today — admission, district nurse, anything.

cues: June's hands shake as she steadies the phone.
June mentions "a strong smell" when helping Edith to the toilet.
The kettle behind them has visible burn marks.

checkpoints.text: Considers delirium first (UTI / opiate toxicity / dehydration / electrolytes) — not dementia by default

Gathers what a video allows — observes Edith, cognitive screen (4AT/AMTS questions over video), asks June for the home BP/temperature readings — and arranges same-day in-person review for examination + urinalysis
Sends urine MSU; arranges bloods (U&Es, FBC, CRP, glucose, calcium, B12/folate, TSH)
Reviews co-codamol — stops or reduces; considers laxative cover
Acknowledges June's exhaustion and asks how SHE is, not only about mother
Speaks directly to Edith (not over her), assesses capacity for the decisions at hand
Considers carer support — respite, social services referral, GP carer review for June
Safety-nets: when to call 999 (drowsy, fitting, sudden deterioration) vs surgery (worsening confusion, falls)

worked.txt: "June — before I talk to your mum, tell me what's happened in the last fortnight, in your own words?"
"Edith — I'm Dr Patel, can you see me alright? Your daughter's been worried about you. Tell me how you've been."
"The very rapid change over two weeks tells me this might not be the dementia getting worse — it can be something else on top, often something we can treat."
"June — I want to ask about you, not just your mum. When did you last have a night off?"
"If she becomes drowsy, has a fit, or her breathing changes — that's 999. If she gets more confused or has another fall — ring us."

f.learning: A fortnight of new confusion in an older adult is delirium until proven otherwise — the screen is UTI, drugs (opiates), dehydration, infection, electrolytes. The hidden examiner agenda here is the carer: spotting June's burden and offering her something IS the consultation's Relating-to-Others mark.

knowledge.guideline: NICE CG103 — Delirium · NICE guidance — Delirium
knowledge.summary: New, fluctuating confusion over days–weeks in an older adult is delirium until proven otherwise — screen for the precipitant rather than defaulting to “worsening dementia”.

points.t: Delirium: acute/subacute onset, fluctuating, impaired attention, often reversible. Use 4AT to assess. A two-week change on a background of mild memory impairment = delirium first.

Pain, Infection (UTI/chest), Nutrition/dehydration, Constipation, Hydration, Medication (opioids — here co-codamol), Environment — plus electrolytes on bloods. Do not use a urine dipstick to diagnose UTI in an older person; treat the patient, not the dipstick.

Obs (incl. temperature, sats, NEWS2) and capillary glucose, hydration, focal neurology, abdomen/bladder, medication review, cognitive screen; bloods (U&E, FBC, CRP, LFTs, glucose, calcium, TFTs, B12/folate given her memory background); urine culture only if urinary symptoms or suspected sepsis without another source.
Address Edith directly, assess capacity for the decisions in hand (MCA — assume capacity, decision-specific), act in best interests if she lacks it.

points.h: The carer is part of the consultation
points.t: Identify carer strain (June): offer a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014), respite, GP carer review, and support — this carries real Relating-to-Others marks.
999 for drowsiness, seizure, sudden deterioration; clear plan for who to call and when, and consider whether home management is safe vs admission.

model.text: Hello Edith, I’m Dr Singh — lovely to meet you. (To daughter) And you must be June. Thank you both for calling. June, would you tell me what’s been worrying you?
model.why: Engages both patient and carer, open question

model.text: (June) She’s just not herself, doctor. Muddled, forgetting things, not eating. Over the last fortnight. She’s never been this bad.
That must be frightening to watch. Edith, may I ask you a few questions directly too — is that alright?
model.why: Includes the patient, not only the carer

model.text: (Edith) If you like, dear. Though I don’t know what all the fuss is about.
June, was this change gradual over months, or did it come on over days?
model.why: Onset/course — the key to separating delirium from dementia

model.text: (June) Quite quick — over a couple of weeks. Some days she’s clearer than others. Mornings are worse.
That fluctuation is really important. Any cough, urine symptoms, fever, or has she had a fall?
(June) No cough. She did have a fall last week, no injury. I don’t know about her waterworks.
And has anything changed with her tablets recently — anything new started?
model.why: Hunts for a precipitant; medication review

model.text: (June) The only new thing is those co-codamol the other doctor gave her for her knee, about four weeks ago.
Thank you — that could be very relevant. How have her bowels been, and is she drinking enough?
(June) Now you mention it, she’s been constipated and barely drinking.
Edith, I’d like to do a quick check — your temperature, pulse, oxygen levels and blood pressure, listen to your chest, feel your tummy, and ask you four short questions. Is that okay?
model.why: Structured assessment incl. obs and a delirium screen (4AT)

model.text: (Edith) Go on then.
(Examines) Her observations are stable, chest is clear, but her tummy’s a little full lower down and she’s dry. On the four questions she’s more muddled than June tells me is normal for her.
I’d also like to send some bloods and a urine sample — to check for infection, kidney function, salts, calcium, sugar and thyroid — so we don’t miss a treatable cause.
June, before I explain — what had you been fearing this was?
model.why: Elicits the carer’s ideas and concerns

model.text: (June) That her dementia’s suddenly got much worse and she can’t stay at home.

I understand why — but I think this is something different and more hopeful. A sudden, fluctuating change like this is usually a delirium: the brain reacting to something physical. Here, the likely culprits are the new co-codamol, constipation and not drinking enough — and importantly, those are treatable.
model.why: Reaches working diagnosis (delirium) and explains it plainly

model.text: (June) Oh — so she might come back to herself?
Very often, yes, once we fix the cause. It’s not the same as her dementia simply stepping down.
model.why: Addresses the carer’s specific fear directly

model.text: So here’s the plan. I’ll stop the co-codamol and switch to regular paracetamol for her knee. We’ll treat the constipation with a laxative, and really focus on fluids. I’ll chase the urine and bloods today. Does that feel manageable between us?
model.why: Treats the precipitants; safe, practical plan

model.text: (June) Yes, I can keep her drinking and sort the laxative.
And June — you’re carrying a lot. You’re entitled to a carer’s assessment for support and respite, and I’d like to arrange that. Caring for someone with delirium is exhausting.
model.why: Recognises carer strain; signposts statutory support

model.text: (June) That would honestly make a difference.
On capacity — Edith can’t fully weigh this up right now, so I’m making these decisions in her best interests, but I’ll keep involving her as she improves.
model.why: Addresses Mental Capacity Act / best interests appropriately

model.text: Safety-net: if she becomes drowsy and hard to rouse, develops a fever, stops drinking altogether, or suddenly worsens, ring us — or 999 if you can’t wake her. I’ll call you this afternoon with the urine result and visit again if needed. What will you do if she becomes very drowsy?
model.why: Clear escalation safety-net and checks understanding

model.text: (June) Call you, or 999 if I can’t wake her. Thank you, doctor — that’s a huge relief.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

Family’s idea (dementia worsening), their concern, and what they hoped for from the visit.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — June is terrified mother will die at home alone before help arrives. She has not slept properly in a fortnight — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

social.t: June is exhausted — offer a Carer’s Assessment under the Care Act 2014, respite and support; carer breakdown is a common reason placement fails.
Hydration, nutrition, falls risk and the practicalities of managing delirium at home shape the home-vs-admission decision.

legal.t: Confusion alone does not remove capacity — assess it for each decision; if Edith lacks it, act in her best interests, least-restrictive option, and involve family. A deprivation of liberty at home needs Court of Protection authorisation (DoLS covers hospitals and care homes only).
Be alert to safeguarding under the Care Act (s42) if neglect or abuse is suspected; check for any LPA for health & welfare.

professional.t: GMC: assess capacity decision-specifically, document it, and make best-interests decisions with those close to her — treating without consent only where she lacks capacity.

community.t: Age UK, Alzheimer’s Society, Admiral Nurses (dementia), local authority social care and carers’ services.

playbook.diagnosis: Distinguish delirium from dementia and give hope: “This sudden, fluctuating change is most likely a delirium — the brain reacting to something physical — and those triggers are treatable, so she may well come back to herself.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This isn’t her dementia suddenly jumping ahead. Her brain is reacting to physical things — a strong new painkiller, constipation and not drinking enough — a bit like a phone glitching when it overheats. Cool it down and it usually works again.”

management.psychosocial: Treat June as the second patient — offer a Carer’s Assessment (Care Act 2014), respite and support; build a plan that keeps Edith safely at home if June can be supported.
sharedPlan: Treat precipitants: stop co-codamol → paracetamol, laxative, hydration; urinalysis + bloods (FBC, U&E, CRP, glucose, calcium, B12/folate, TSH)
Decide home vs admission on safety; act in best interests (MCA) as she lacks capacity now, involving family

pitfalls.intro: The two ways to fail this visit: accept “her dementia has got worse”, and spend twelve minutes talking to the daughter about a patient sitting in the same room.

items.fail: Accepting the family’s framing — worsening dementia — and consulting about long-term care.
items.why: “Failure to generate the correct hypothesis.” A two-week, fluctuating change with poor attention is delirium until proven otherwise; missing it is a patient-safety-level error.
items.fix: Name the distinction early and out loud: sudden + fluctuating + inattentive = delirium (use the 4AT) — “and delirium has a findable, treatable cause”.

items.fail: Dipstick says leucocytes, so it’s “a UTI” — trimethoprim prescribed, visit over.
items.why: “Managed the dipstick, not the patient.” UK guidance is explicit that urine dips mislead in the over-65s — while the real precipitants (a four-week-old co-codamol, constipation, dehydration) sit in the stem.
items.fix: Work PINCH ME aloud — Pain, INfection, Constipation, deHydration, Medication, Electrolytes — and review the drug chart first: the co-codamol is the prime suspect.

items.fail: The entire visit conducted with June while Edith is talked about in the third person.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient.” Deferring to family is respectful in many of the systems candidates trained in — in the SCA, the patient is addressed directly whatever her cognition.
items.fix: Sit at her level, introduce yourself to Edith first, direct questions to her, and signpost the collateral: “I’ll check some details with your daughter — but I want to hear from you.”

items.fail: Capacity handled by assumption — either “she’s confused, so the daughter decides”, or asking Edith to hold complex decisions she cannot.
items.why: “Did not address capacity correctly.” The MCA is decision-specific: assume capacity until assessed otherwise, then best interests and the least-restrictive option.
items.fix: Assess capacity for each specific decision (bloods, staying home tonight), narrate your reasoning, and involve June in best interests rather than as the decision-maker.

items.fail: June’s “I can’t do this much longer” answered with “you’re doing a great job” — and nothing else.
items.why: “Cue acknowledged but not acted on.” Carer strain is a scored item; the Care Act carer’s assessment exists for exactly this moment.
items.fix: Offer the concrete thing: a carer’s assessment, respite options, and a named follow-up — “you’re a patient in this too, not just the help.”

items.fail: The visit ends with bloods sent and no judgement on whether home is safe tonight.
items.why: “Management plan incomplete / no safety-netting.” Delirium at home demands an explicit home-versus-admission decision with escalation triggers.
items.fix: State the judgement and the triggers: who stays with her, what June watches for — drowsiness, not drinking, falls, seizure — and exactly when it is 999 versus the surgery.

timeMap.d: June starts the call with Edith beside her. Hear her fortnight in her own words — then greet Edith directly, by name, on screen.

Delirium screen, not dementia assumptions: timeline, fluctuation, urine symptoms, fluids, the NEW co-codamol, the fall. Gather what video allows (observation, 4AT questions, home readings via June) and arrange same-day in-person examination + urinalysis.
"A two-week change this fast is usually something ON TOP of memory problems — often an infection or a medicine — and those we can treat."
MSU + bloods today; stop/reduce co-codamol; fluids plan; admission threshold stated. Then the second patient: "June — when did you last have a night off?" Carer referral.
999: drowsy, fitting, sudden deterioration. Surgery: more confused, another fall. Write it down — a frightened carer at 2am needs paper, not memory.

wordPics.fail: Accepts "dementia getting worse" and refers to memory clinic routinely; never reviews the new co-codamol; talks over Edith to the daughter throughout the call; June's exhaustion is never asked about; no same-day investigations despite a 2-week acute change.
wordPics.pass: Treats it as delirium until proven otherwise; examines and sends MSU/bloods; reviews and stops the opioid; speaks to Edith directly at least some of the time; gives a 999-vs-surgery safety-net; mentions support for June.
wordPics.exc: Runs the full delirium screen including drugs and dehydration; assesses Edith's capacity for today's decisions while keeping her dignity; explicitly makes June a patient too — carer review, respite referral, acknowledges the pension top-ups; leaves a written plan with explicit escalation triggers.

avoid.dont: (To the daughter, over Edith's head) "How long has she been like this?"
avoid.instead: "Edith — I'm the doctor, I've come to see you. Tell me how you've been." (Then cross-check with June.)
avoid.why: Talking over the patient is a Relating-to-Others fail you can't recover from.

avoid.dont: "It sounds like her dementia is progressing — I'll refer her to the memory clinic."
avoid.instead: "A change this quick is usually delirium — something treatable sitting on top. Let's find it before we re-label her memory."
avoid.why: Dementia-by-default misses the reversible cause — the entire point of the station.

avoid.dont: "You're doing a wonderful job — keep it up."
avoid.instead: "June, I want to ask about you, not just your mum. When did you last sleep through? There is real help I can set up this week."
avoid.why: Praise without action abandons the carer; the carer IS the hidden agenda.

social.t: June is exhausted — offer a Carer’s Assessment under the Care Act 2014, respite and support; carer breakdown is a common reason placement fails.
Hydration, nutrition, falls risk and the practicalities of managing delirium at home shape the home-vs-admission decision.

legal.t: Confusion alone does not remove capacity — assess it for each decision; if Edith lacks it, act in her best interests, least-restrictive option, and involve family. A deprivation of liberty at home needs Court of Protection authorisation (DoLS covers hospitals and care homes only).
Be alert to safeguarding under the Care Act (s42) if neglect or abuse is suspected; check for any LPA for health & welfare.

professional.t: GMC: assess capacity decision-specifically, document it, and make best-interests decisions with those close to her — treating without consent only where she lacks capacity.

community.t: Age UK, Alzheimer’s Society, Admiral Nurses (dementia), local authority social care and carers’ services.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Distinguish delirium from dementia and give hope: “This sudden, fluctuating change is most likely a delirium — the brain reacting to something physical — and those triggers are treatable, so she may well come back to herself.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “This isn’t her dementia suddenly jumping ahead. Her brain is reacting to physical things — a strong new painkiller, constipation and not drinking enough — a bit like a phone glitching when it overheats. Cool it down and it usually works again.”

management.reflectIce: “I know you feared this was her dementia stepping down a level for good — I think it’s something different and more hopeful, and that once we fix the cause she should improve.”
management.psychosocial: Treat June as the second patient — offer a Carer’s Assessment (Care Act 2014), respite and support; build a plan that keeps Edith safely at home if June can be supported.
sharedPlan: Treat precipitants: stop co-codamol → paracetamol, laxative, hydration; urinalysis + bloods (FBC, U&E, CRP, glucose, calcium, B12/folate, TSH)
Decide home vs admission on safety; act in best interests (MCA) as she lacks capacity now, involving family
safetyNet: Drowsy/unrousable, fever, stops drinking, sudden worsening → call us or 999
Chase urine/bloods today; planned review or revisit

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The two ways to fail this visit: accept “her dementia has got worse”, and spend twelve minutes talking to the daughter about a patient sitting in the same room.

items.fail: Accepting the family’s framing — worsening dementia — and consulting about long-term care.
items.why: “Failure to generate the correct hypothesis.” A two-week, fluctuating change with poor attention is delirium until proven otherwise; missing it is a patient-safety-level error.
items.fix: Name the distinction early and out loud: sudden + fluctuating + inattentive = delirium (use the 4AT) — “and delirium has a findable, treatable cause”.

items.fail: Dipstick says leucocytes, so it’s “a UTI” — trimethoprim prescribed, visit over.
items.why: “Managed the dipstick, not the patient.” UK guidance is explicit that urine dips mislead in the over-65s — while the real precipitants (a four-week-old co-codamol, constipation, dehydration) sit in the stem.
items.fix: Work PINCH ME aloud — Pain, INfection, Constipation, deHydration, Medication, Electrolytes — and review the drug chart first: the co-codamol is the prime suspect.

items.fail: The entire visit conducted with June while Edith is talked about in the third person.
items.why: “Did not involve the patient.” Deferring to family is respectful in many of the systems candidates trained in — in the SCA, the patient is addressed directly whatever her cognition.
items.fix: Sit at her level, introduce yourself to Edith first, direct questions to her, and signpost the collateral: “I’ll check some details with your daughter — but I want to hear from you.”

items.fail: Capacity handled by assumption — either “she’s confused, so the daughter decides”, or asking Edith to hold complex decisions she cannot.
items.why: “Did not address capacity correctly.” The MCA is decision-specific: assume capacity until assessed otherwise, then best interests and the least-restrictive option.
items.fix: Assess capacity for each specific decision (bloods, staying home tonight), narrate your reasoning, and involve June in best interests rather than as the decision-maker.

items.fail: June’s “I can’t do this much longer” answered with “you’re doing a great job” — and nothing else.
items.why: “Cue acknowledged but not acted on.” Carer strain is a scored item; the Care Act carer’s assessment exists for exactly this moment.
items.fix: Offer the concrete thing: a carer’s assessment, respite options, and a named follow-up — “you’re a patient in this too, not just the help.”

items.fail: The visit ends with bloods sent and no judgement on whether home is safe tonight.
items.why: “Management plan incomplete / no safety-netting.” Delirium at home demands an explicit home-versus-admission decision with escalation triggers.
items.fix: State the judgement and the triggers: who stays with her, what June watches for — drowsiness, not drinking, falls, seizure — and exactly when it is 999 versus the surgery.
